description: We’re Sur Zameen, a duo from Karachi combining code and storytelling. We’re building an Earth Jukebox that turns NASA Earth data into real-time sound, mapping climate variables to South Asian classical raag scales so people can hear the planet change. It also opens up Earth science to blind and low-vision audiences.
summary: Sur Zameen is an Earth Jukebox that lets people hear NASA Earth data. Using NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio night-lights animation (Black Marble / VIIRS, 2012–2023), we measure each frame’s mean brightness, share of bright pixels and change from the previous frame, then play those numbers as Raag Yaman, tuned in just intonation over a synthesized drone. Brighter frames climb higher, a larger share of bright pixels means denser notes, and bigger frame-to-frame change shortens notes and speeds the glides. A finale plays an ascending phrase because purple (more light) pixels outnumber orange (less light) in the change map. Because Earth science is mostly shown visually, sound opens it to blind and low-vision users: full keyboard control, screen-reader descriptions and an audio-only mode are built in.
details:
What it does: Sur Zameen is an “Earth Jukebox” that lets people hear NASA Earth data. It pairs frames from NASA’s night-lights animation with sound generated live in the browser, so Earth science doesn’t have to be seen to be understood.

How it works: We extracted frames from NASA SVS #5313, “Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023, EIC Version,” with FFmpeg. A Python script (NumPy, Pillow) measures 10 curated frames from the night-lights series: mean brightness, share of pixels above a brightness threshold, and change from the previous frame. Transition frames and the regional zoom insets were excluded. Frames 12 to 21 of the change map are collapsed into one finale record: the share of purple pixels (more light) and orange pixels (less light), measured at about 2.8 to 1. Because differences between frames are small, we normalize each metric across the sequence, so the music shows relative change within the animation, not absolute light levels.

The numbers drive music in Raag Yaman, tuned in just intonation (pure ratios, not piano tuning). Brightness picks the note, the bright-pixel share sets note density (1, 2 or 3 notes per frame), and frame-to-frame change sets note length and glide (meend). Every value snaps to the nearest note in the raag, so the same data always gives the same music. The finale plays an ascending phrase because purple outnumbers orange in our count. The page lists each mapping and shows the note and frequency being played.

Accessibility: Full keyboard control (Space, arrows, D for the drone, V for audio-only), a screen-reader description that updates for each frame, visible focus outlines, and an audio-only mode.

Built with: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Tone.js (Web Audio), Python, NumPy, Pillow, FFmpeg, Google Fonts, GitHub Pages. The drone and melody are synthesized in the browser. No recorded samples are used.

Limits: Our metrics come from our own pixel measurements of the animation frames, not NASA’s raw radiance data. The frame-to-frame differences are small, and the purple/orange count is approximate.
